sources.text:
* 1\. Ring: This architecture is commonly seen in pre-aggregation and aggregation networks where traffic is being collected and aggregated from the access towards components in the aggregation or transport core. Connectivity between routers is either via direct dark fibre connections or via lambdas derived from a WDM system.
  * 2\. Dual hub and spoke: This architecture is most commonly seen in aggregation and core transport networks but also sometimes in pre-aggregation networks. It is used to collect and aggregate traffic towards common aggregation points. Connectivity between routers is typically via direct dark fibre or via lambdas derived from a WDM system.
  * Note: Hub and spoke architectures are often super-imposed over a physical ring topology using WDM technology.
  * 3\. Mesh: This is architecture is normally seen in transport core networks but can be seen in aggregation networks. It is used when traffic is flowing in an any-to-any fashion. As drive distances increase and connectivity becomes meshier in nature, so there is increasing use of DWDM and ROADM technology to derive the links between routers.

sources.text:
* Section 7 outlines the 5G interfaces the transport network needs to support. In many areas the transport QoS requirements for 5G are very similar to existing 4G and general multi-service environments. However, there are some notable considerations and exceptions.
  * In the context of packet-based switching technologies for O-RAN and 3GPP, the interplay of QoS and transport slicing has two dimensions: 1\) The QoS requirements of O-RAN fronthaul traffic 2\) The QoS requirements of the mobile services, which depends on the kind of application being delivered to the end users. The transport slicing and QoS architectures needs to consider both dimensions to properly allocate QoS resources capable of satisfying the expected requirements for each kind of traffic in terms of bandwidth, latency, etc.
  * O-RAN 7.2X Fronthaul Traffic: The user and control traffic stream is eCPRI based and runs between the O-RU and the O-DU. It is a new traffic type associated with 5G. The transport requirements of the Fronthaul user and control plane interfaces are contained in the O- RAN.WG9.CTRP-REQ-V01.00 \[20\] but can be summarised as high bandwidth and more importantly from a QoS perspective, extremely low delay \(micro-seconds\) traffic. Due to the low delay requirements this traffic type will only ever be seen in the access network and requires packet switching equipment to treat this traffic with the highest priority through the device and when scheduling onto attached interfaces. Today, many Service Providers use the highest priority queue for voice traffic, consequently, changes to the existing QoS schemes may be required.
  * 5G introduces Midhaul: Midhaul interfaces run between the O-DUs and the O-CUs and between O-CUs. The F1 interfaces are a new set of interfaces associated with 5G, but use GTP-U and GTP-C which is the same packet types used in Backhaul. It is expected that Midhaul and Backhaul interfaces will have similar QoS requirements.
  * 5G introduces new service types, each with their own QoS requirements. GTPv1-U \[5\] is used in the Midhaul and Backhaul for F1-U, Xn-U, N3 and N9 interfaces. The importance of user data packet within the mobile environment is indicated in the QoS Field Identifier \(QFI\)Error\! Reference source not found. in the GTP-U extension header\[5\]. High performance TNEs do not have the capability to examine the QFI field and instead use the DSCP field in the IP header or the MPLS Traffic Class to understand the QoS requirements of packets in the transport network. For the transport network to be able to treat GTP-U packets in an appropriate fashion for the mobile service, the Midhaul \(starting from O-RAN slicing phase 2\) and Backhaul \(starting from O-RAN slicing phase 1\) mobile components \(O-DUs, O-CU-UP and UPFs\) must have mechanisms to set a DSCP value in the GTP IP header appropriate to the QoS requirements of the mobile service carried in the GTP-U packet. This could be achieved using a mapping mechanism on the Midhaul and Backhaul mobile components that map QFI values to DSCP values.

options: 2. To connect O-CUs to the core network.
3. To connect user devices to the network.
4. To connect O-DUs to the user devices.

sources.text:
* 1\. O-DUs connect, via Ethernet interface/interfaces, to a co-located HSR or CSR. The Ethernet interface/interfaces support Midhaul control and user plane traffic via two discrete VLANs.
  * 2\. O-CUs connect, via Ethernet interfaces to the transport network. The O-CU Ethernet interface/interfaces support Midhaul and Backhaul control and user plane traffic via two discrete VLANs.
  * 3\. The UPFs connect, via Ethernet interfaces to the transport network. The UPF connects to the common control and user plane Midhaul/Backhaul VPNs.
  * 4\. The location of the O-CUs and UPFs is service dependent and the choice of the operator. Additionally, these components may be virtualized or containerized and reside in a data center. In these scenarios, orchestration techniques maybe be required to connect the virtualized O-DU, O-CU and UPF components in the data centers to the correct WAN L3VPNs.
  * 5\. 5G Core components connect via Ethernet interfaces to the transport network in their respective locations. These components may be virtualized or containerized and reside in a data center. In these scenarios, orchestration techniques are required to connect the 5G control plane entities in the data centers to the Midhaul and Backhaul control plane WAN L3VPNs.

sources.text:
* In slicing phase 1 slicing is not supported on Midhaul O-RAN mobile components. O-DUs and O-
  * CU-UPs do not have a concept of slicing with the F1-U traffic from all slices originating and
  * terminating on the same physical/logical interface and IP address on the O-DU. In scenarios, where
  * the O-CU-UP is shared between two or more slices there is also no concept of slicing on the O-CU-
  * UP. In situations, as shown in Figure 26-2, where the O-CU-UP is dedicated to a slice, then the O-
  * CU-UP function will only receive and send traffic associated with that slice, however the O-CU-UP
  * slice assignment and selection process is completely transparent to the transport network and under
  * the control of the O-RAN / 3GPP control planes. For this reason, in slicing phase 1 a single MP-
  * BGP L3VPN mapped to the underlay's default routing algorithm is used across the transport
  * network to support all Midhaul user plane traffic regardless of slice it belongs too. The L3VPN
  * needs to be present on all TNEs and DC-TNEs that either connect directly or indirectly \(through the
  * DC infrastructure\) to mobile components that support Midhaul user plane interfaces. Access to the
  * Midhaul user plane VPN, on the TNEs, is via VLAN interfaces.
  * A further challenge with Midhaul user plane interfaces in slicing phase 1 is the lack of a QoS
  * mapping function on the O-DUs to map radio orientated QoS parameters, controlled by the 3GPP /
  * ORAN control planes, to transport orientated DSCP QoS markings. The means the transport
  * network QoS mechanisms must treat all uplink traffic the same, regardless of the importance of the
  * data contained within Midhaul GTP-U packets.
  * Slicing Phase 2 and 3
  * Midhaul slicing and QoS is supported in slicing phase 2 and 3. F1-U traffic segregation is supported
  * using a VLAN per user plane slice on the O-DUs and O-CU-UPs and QoS is supported by the O-
  * DUs and O-CU-UPs setting a DSCP value appropriate to the importance of the user payload in the
  * GTP-U packet.

details.question: What is the main benefit of utilizing a uniform network model in an O-RAN architecture?
options: 1.  Simplifies network management by providing a consistent view of the network.
2.  Enables seamless integration of different vendor technologies.
3.  Reduces complexity and duplicate work in the upper layers.

sources.text: Utilizing a uniform network model brings the benefit of keeping the complexity as low as possible in the hierarchy, as well as avoiding duplicate work in the upper layers. It can be regarded as a service responsible for presenting a uniform network model to any other application or service interested, while translating or mapping the underlying device YANG models. An example of how such a service could fit into the controller architecture is depicted in Figure B.1.3-2.
sources.trace: B.1Network Slicing Use Case --> B.1.3 Uniform transport network model

sources.text: As seen in Figure B.1.3.1-1, the abstract topology model can be used to define layer specific, service or usecase specific topology models. Concerning the uniform network model, such a generic model without the specifics of a particular inventory/topology types allows to present an aggregated and uniform network view without needing to provide any device related specifics. It could be also easier not only to describe multilayer topologies but also multi-domain topologies w.r.t nodes and links. Furthermore, IETF provides different data models for different network layers such as RFC 8944 for Layer 2 and RFC 8346 for Layer 3 topologies. All these models are derived from the same ietf-network-topology which will technically make it easier for their augmentation into the same topology model when it comes to providing a uniform network view.
sources.trace: B.1Network Slicing Use Case --> B.1.3 Uniform transport network model --> B.1.3.1Multi-domain Support

sources.text: In this way, the uniform network model could enable network slicing through a unified view of the underlying end-to-end network, as well as other use cases, such as AI/ML applications, Closed Loop use cases or Data Lakes that leverage a uniform end-to-end network view.
sources.trace: B.1Network Slicing Use Case --> B.1.3 Uniform transport network model

sources.text: This chapter elaborates the concept of the uniform network model and the benefits it brings in moderating the complexity of network control and management when it comes to creating connectivity services or network slices across domains following different standards and device models. As a starting point, this chapter includes a brief overview of our survey on the topological model of two standards namely T-API and IETF and possibilities of utilizing them for the uniform network view. As a result, it has been highlighted that T-API and its supported interface profiles have a strong hold on optical domain. IETF on the other hand, supports diverse interface profiles from different domains, hence, can be considered as a better choice. A high-level architecture of the Abstraction Layer is introduced in this phase with a brief explanation of the possible components in this layer. As part of this concept, two approaches of constructing the unified device information model have been proposed. In the next phases, an examination of different models from different domains will be performed in order to understand the existing gaps and also the feasibility of reusing the existing models when it comes to constructing the uniform network model.

details.question: What is the primary function of the Open Xhaul transport network in an O-RAN architecture?
options: 1. Providing connectivity between the RAN and the mobile packet core.
2. Enabling communication between user equipment and the gNB.
3. Managing the flow of data between the UPF and the gNB.
4. Securing the connection between the RAN and the internet.

sources.text: Figure 8 shows the NSA option 3/3a/3x networking modes. In NSA option 3 \(far left in figure\) the signalling and user plane traffic associated with 5G UEs is sent from gNBs to eNBs and then onto the mobile core. In this mode, traffic levels between the gNB and the eNB and between the eNB and the EPC are a function of the amount of 5G spectrum and the number of 5G UEs. It is anticipated traffic levels will initially be low due to the scarcity of 5G UEs but could become very significant as the user population transitions towards 5G UEs and gets the benefits of increased capacity from using 5G NR. This mode impacts the transport infrastructure between the gNB and the eNB and also the transport infrastructure between the eNB and the EPC.

sources.text: The data network or N6 is not part of the RAN and is not in scope of the WG-1 slicing work item. However, transport slicing needs to extend to the N6 data network, particularly as the Data Network \(N6\) network extends closer to the radio infrastructure with multiple breakout points and although not discussed in this annex, the techniques outlined for the backhaul and midhaul user plane slicing are largely applicable when building the data networks across a common packet switched transport infrastructure. An important consideration when utilising multiple breakout points in the data network \(N6\) is to ensure traffic exits the network in the desired place but also returning traffic enters the data network \(N6\) in desired place. This requires UPF address block planning within the data network, how these routes are advertised externally by the routers at the peering points and how external routes are advertised within the Data network \(N6\).

details.question: What is the primary function of a PRTC (Primary Reference Time Clock) in an O-RAN network?
options: 1. To provide a reference signal for the timing or synchronization of other clocks within a network.
2. To deliver a primary time reference for time and/or phase synchronization by other clocks in the network.
3. To maintain the local representation of the timescale during outages of the input time reference.
4. To provide a frequency input reference traceable to a PRC.

details.question: Which protocol is used for the transport layer in O-RAN, providing reliable and ordered delivery of data?

sources.text: The Transport Network Layer is based on IP transport, comprising the SCTP on top of IP. SCTP \(IETF RFC 4960 \[9\] \) shall be supported as the transport layer of D2-c control bearer \(D2CP\). SCTP refers to the Stream Control Transmission Protocol developed by the Sigtran working group of the IETF for the purpose of transporting various signalling protocols over IP network. There shall be only one SCTP association established between two O-DUs. No SCTP Destination Port number value was assigned by IANA for the D2CP protocol and so networks shall rely on O-DU configuration to select a suitable port number.
sources.trace: 7 D2 application protocol structure --> 7.1 D2 control plane protocol \(D2-c\)

sources.text: The application layer signalling protocol is referred to as D2CP \(D2 Control Protocol\). The Payload Protocol Identifier assigned by IANA to be used by SCTP for the application layer protocol D2CP is 71. This value is to be used for all deployment configurations described in the present document. The byte order of the Payload Protocol Identifier shall be bigendian. The O-DUs shall support a configuration with a single SCTP association per O-DU pair.

sources.text: The active WDM equipment can send management requests to the O-RU and manage the WDM optical modules within the O-RU, including query and configuration. The optical modules within the O-RU can receive management requests from the active WDM equipment and then send the OAM information of the optical modules to the active WDM equipment, including the wavelength and output power of the transmitter. The optical modules in the O-RU and the O-DU can send the OAM information of optical modules to the active WDM equipment automatically or at regular time intervals once the optical modules are powered on. The WDM optical modules can add the OAM information with the service signals and transport them together in the same optical channel. The detection unit in the active WDM equipment can demodulate the OAM information, obtain the transmission performance of O-RU and O-DU, and then report it to the control system through the standard southbound interface. The semi-active WDM type I equipment should support query, configuration, and send OAM information. To further reduce system cost, the semi-active WDM type II equipment can perform simplified management, including sending the OAM information of optical modules to the active WDM equipment.
